findings.title: Queue pool is permanently shut down on the first rebalance, then reused
findings.body: `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` hands the single, factory-owned `self.queue_pool` to every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` it creates. Arroyo closes the strategy on every partition revocation/rebalance, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which stops all worker threads and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue. The factory still holds a non-None reference, so the next `create_with_partitions()` after the rebalance returns a strategy backed by a dead pool: `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which is swallowed by the `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()`, where the offset is immediately marked added+complete and therefore committed. The result is that after the first rebalance the consumer silently drops every message while advancing offsets, i.e. permanent data loss. The pool needs to be created per strategy (or recreated on assignment) rather than shared across the factory lifetime.

findings.title: Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread
findings.body: `_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `Commit` callback (`StreamProcessor.__commit` -> `consumer.stage_offsets`/`commit_offsets`). That callback and the underlying consumer state are only safe to touch from the thread running the processor loop; calling it concurrently with `poll()`/`submit()`/rebalance handling can corrupt the staged-offset bookkeeping or raise (e.g. staging an offset for a partition that was just revoked). Because the exception is caught and only logged in the loop, such failures would be invisible and offsets would silently stop advancing. Offsets should be handed back to the main thread (e.g. collected in `poll()`) instead of committed from the commit thread.

findings.title: Shutdown drops all queued work instead of draining it; join() ignores timeout
findings.body: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` *before* calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Each worker checks `self.shutdown` at the top of its loop, so after finishing its current item it exits immediately and never drains the remaining queued items, defeating the point of `immediate=False`. Combined with `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` which just delegates to `close()` and ignores the timeout entirely, a normal shutdown or rebalance discards everything still queued. Those offsets stay uncommitted so the messages are re-delivered, but arroyo's `join(timeout)` contract (flush outstanding work within the timeout) is broken and every restart/rebalance causes a burst of duplicate processing proportional to the queue depth.

findings.title: Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the docstring claim
findings.body: Each queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring of `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever fills up: if a result processor is slower than the Kafka consumption rate, the strategy will keep accepting messages and grow memory without bound. Each `WorkItem` also retains the full `Message[KafkaPayload]` (field `message`, which is never read anywhere), so the retained payload bytes are kept alive as well, plus one entry per offset in `OffsetTracker.all_offsets`. A bounded queue plus `MessageRejected` (or an explicit limit) is needed to get real backpressure.

findings.title: OffsetTracker state is never reset across partition assignments
findings.body: `OffsetTracker` lives on the long-lived `FixedQueuePool` and keeps `last_committed`/`all_offsets` forever; `create_with_partitions()` never resets it for the newly assigned partition set. If a partition is revoked and later re-assigned to this consumer at a lower offset (rewind, other consumer committed less far, offset reset), `get_committable_offsets()` computes `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` from the stale `last_committed`, finds no offsets at or above it, and therefore never produces a committable offset for that partition again - the consumer processes messages but silently stops committing, so the lag grows without bound and everything is reprocessed on restart. The tracker should be reset (or scoped per assignment) when partitions are assigned/revoked.

findings.title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of the implemented behaviour and passes only by timing
findings.body: `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` is documented as "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages" but then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that nothing is committed. In the implementation the worker catches the exception and still calls `complete_offset()` in its `finally` block, so offsets 100 and 101 become committable and the 1-second commit loop will commit them. The test only passes because its wait loop exits after ~0.3s, before the first commit tick. So it asserts behaviour the code does not have, is timing-dependent (will fail whenever the commit thread ticks early / CI is slow), and provides no real coverage of failure handling.

findings.title: Offset-gap test does not actually verify gap blocking and is timing-dependent
findings.body: `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` submits offsets 100, 102, 103 and asserts that no commit ever exceeds 101. The tracker blocks at the gap only for the first commit tick: after `mark_committed(100)` removes offsets <= 100, the next call to `get_committable_offsets()` uses `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset) = 102` and will therefore commit 103 (reported as 104). The test passes only because the wait loop breaks ~0.2s after the first commit, before the next 1-second tick, making it flaky; and the `for commit in all_commits: assert <= 101` loop gives a false sense that committing past gaps is prevented. Either the skip-the-gap behaviour should be asserted explicitly, or the loop should keep observing commits for more than one tick.

findings.title: Strategy docstring guarantees do not match behaviour
findings.body: The `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring claims "No item is lost or processed out of order", "Natural backpressure when queues fill up" and "Only commits offsets after successful processing". None of those hold: queues are unbounded (no backpressure), items still queued at close are discarded, and the worker marks an offset complete in its `finally` block even when `result_processor` raised, so failed items are committed and never retried. Leaving these claims in place will mislead operators about the delivery semantics of the new mode.

findings.title: FilteredPayload messages are funneled through the generic exception handler
findings.body: `ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload` starts with `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`, and that assert is outside its try/except. When this strategy is wrapped by something that emits `FilteredPayload` (e.g. the stale-message DLQ wrapper used via `--stale-threshold-sec`), every filtered message raises an AssertionError that lands in `submit()`'s `except Exception`, logging "Error submitting message to queue" at exception level for each one. Offsets are still advanced, so this is noise rather than data loss, but it will flood error logs/Sentry. `submit()` should handle `FilteredPayload` explicitly (track and complete the offset) instead of relying on the catch-all.
